title: What does the GENIUS Act require of permitted payment stablecoin issuers?
abstract: Sourced guide to the US GENIUS Act: who may issue payment stablecoins, the reserve and redemption rules, monthly disclosure, the ban on paying interest and when it applies.
body:
According to Public Law 119-27, the GENIUS Act defines a permitted payment stablecoin issuer as a US-formed subsidiary of an insured bank approved to issue, a Federal qualified issuer, or a State qualified issuer. The Act was approved on 18 July 2025. [1]

Section 4 requires an issuer to maintain identifiable reserves backing its outstanding payment stablecoins on an at least 1 to 1 basis. The listed reserve assets include United States coins and currency, demand deposits within limits, and Treasury bills, notes or bonds with a remaining maturity of 93 days or less. [1]

The issuer must publish the monthly composition of its reserves on its website, must publicly disclose a redemption policy with clear and conspicuous procedures for timely redemption, and may not pay the holder any form of interest or yield solely in connection with holding, using or retaining the stablecoin. The Act takes effect on the earlier of 18 months after enactment or 120 days after the primary federal regulators issue final regulations. [1]

Author interpretation: the Act defines who may issue a payment stablecoin and what the issuer must hold and disclose, not what a wallet or an agent application must do. A payment service should check who issues each token it uses instead of assuming a token is covered. Sources accessed 11 November 2026. [1]
